reviewed: sources/puredarwin-m1-desktop/src/Kernel/Extensions/IOHIDFamily/IOHIDSystem/PDHIDEventQueue.cpp (sha256 c7a2f35bd86bc2da), plus its callers in IOHIDFamily/IOHIDEventService.cpp (PDHIDPushKeyboardEvent :1795, PDHIDPush[Absolute]MouseEvent :82/:104)
purpose: Pitfalls for Astra's isolated native keyboard endpoint publication/serialization patch (integrations/puredarwin/m1-native-input). Baseline facts only; the frozen patch gets its own review.
baseline_facts: Lazy publication: nodes are created only when the first event arrives. PDHIDPushKeyboardEvent calls PDHIDPublishKeyboardDevice when gKbdLock is NULL, and the mouse enqueue does the same. This is why the host runs needed priming lines.

PDHIDPublish*Device runs from up to three contexts with no lock: the HID event push path, the IOBSD gIOPublishNotification handler, and the 1 s retry thread_call. Each step is check-then-act on globals (gKbdMajor, gKbdNode, gPS2KbdNode, gKbdBSDNotifier, gKbdRetryCall; mouse equivalents).
Keyboard setup swaps gKbdLock, gLEDLock and gConsoleCall in by CAS. The mouse path assigns gMouseLock = IOLockAlloc() without CAS.
PDHIDPushKeyboardEvent assigns event.sequence = ++gKbdSequence before taking gKbdLock. The mouse path increments its sequence under gMouseLock.

Reads return EAGAIN when empty, even for blocking readers. There is no select/kqueue (eno_select). Overflow advances the read index, which wipes the oldest events and leaves a sequence gap; the compositor decoder treats a gap as fatal.
Nodes are created 0666 root:wheel. Any open of usb_hid_kbd sets gKbdGrabbed, which suppresses printable console forwarding until the last close.
The console path is sound: bytes are queued under gKbdLock and drained by gConsoleCall, which calls cons_cinput outside the lock. LED handlers, however, are called while holding gLEDLock.

pitfalls.text: The publish state machine is unserialised. Two concurrent publishers (push path plus notifier or retry) can both cdevsw_add, leaking a major and overwriting gKbdMajor; both devfs_make_node the same name (the second fails and keeps retrying, or a node can point at a stale major); register two IOBSD notifiers; and allocate two retry thread_calls in schedule_retry (*call is not CAS'd, so one leaks and both get scheduled). Use one lock (or a CAS'd state enum) for the whole publication state, allocate the lock once at module or driver start (not lazily from a push), and make every step idempotent under that lock. Fix the non-CAS gMouseLock as well: two concurrent first pushes could create two locks and split the queue.

Never publish from the event push path. In the baseline, the first PDHIDPushKeyboardEvent can call cdevsw_add, devfs_make_node (which takes the devfs mutex and allocates), addMatchingNotification and thread_call_allocate from inside IOHIDEventService dispatch. That is typically the event driver's workloop with its gate held, and for a native SPI keyboard it is inside the driver's report path. Blocking there, or taking IOKit matching or devfs locks under a driver gate, invites deadlock and latency. Publish from a dedicated thread_call scheduled at service or driver start. Until the queue is marked ready, the push path should only enqueue into already-initialised storage (or drop and count), never allocate or publish.

IOService::addMatchingNotification(gIOPublishNotification, resourceMatching('IOBSD')) delivers already-published matches synchronously on the registering thread, before it returns. The baseline handler then re-enters PDHIDPublishKeyboardDevice inside the outer call (recursion). If that inner call creates the node, the handler calls notifier->remove() and tries to clear gKbdBSDNotifier, but the outer call has not stored it yet. The outer call then stores a pointer to the removed (possibly freed) notifier in the global. Make the handler only schedule the publish thread_call (never publish inline, never remove inside the handler), store or remove the notifier only in the owner context under the state lock, and treat the handler firing before registration returns as normal.

Keep both readiness sources (the IOBSD notification and devfs_is_ready), but make the retry bounded and observable. The baseline retries every 1 s forever with no log or state, so a permanently failing devfs_make_node is invisible. Record attempt count and last error, log once on the transition to published and once on giving up, and do not keep retrying a node whose name already exists (EEXIST-like failures). If both a notifier and a retry exist, cancel the other once published. Never create device nodes by any means other than devfs_make_node, and never write to the RAM root's /dev.

Create the node only after every object an open or read can touch is ready: the queue lock, ring indices, console thread_call, LED lock, and for a native endpoint the device binding that will produce events. Publish a 'ready' flag with release ordering after that, and check it in open/read. Opening the keyboard node grabs the console (gKbdGrabbed), so a node that becomes visible before real events can flow lets a compositor steal console input with no source behind it. Visibility must imply that event delivery is wired. Consider defining what open() means when no producer is bound yet (refuse, or allow with an explicit no-producer state) and record it.

Assign event.sequence under gKbdLock in the same critical section that writes the slot, as the mouse path does. With a native keyboard plus PDSerialHID (or two native interfaces) pushing concurrently, the baseline can store sequence N+1 before N, or duplicate values. The compositor decoder then aborts on a discontinuity ('queue overflow or competing reader'). Keep one global ring and one sequence counter per node, both updated under the lock.

LED handlers run while holding gLEDLock on the console thread_call. A native keyboard LED handler that performs a blocking SPI transfer stalls Register/Unregister and other LED updates. A handler that calls PDHIDRegister/UnregisterLEDHandler, or anything that takes gLEDLock, deadlocks (IOLock is not recursive). Unregister does wait for in-flight calls because it takes the same lock, which is good for lifetime. Either document that handlers must be non-blocking and never re-enter, or copy a snapshot of handlers and run them outside gLEDLock with a per-entry reference or quiescence scheme.

The 0666 nodes expose every keystroke to any process and let any process grab console input. That is acceptable in the single-user RAM root, but a native production endpoint should be 0600 root (or a console-user group) and say so. gKbdGrabbed is set on every open and cleared only on the last close (spec_close/vcount), so it is a 'somebody has it open' bit, not a count; keep that semantics explicit if the patch changes open/close.

A published node, an attached service or a successful open is not keyboard evidence. The patch's proof must remain actual native reports (first-report log), real queue records consumed by the compositor, and, for typing, the physical observation rule. No host-origin PDSerialHID lines may be used in a native-keyboard qualification run (keep the old host terminal validation path separate and intact).

not_claimed: any behaviour of the future patch
scope: Read-only baseline source review. No edits, builds or hardware.
